text: will determine the input size. Now, there is an important class of problems where we have to
be a little bit careful about how we talk about input size and these are problems involving numbers.
Suppose we were to write an algorithm for primality checking whether a given number is prime.
Now, how should we think of the size of the input? For instance, suppose we ask it to solve the
question for say 5,000 and three and then for 50,000 and three, then 50,000 and three is roughly
10 times 5,000 and three. So, would be expect the time to grow proportional to 10.
So, should the magnitude of n actually be taken as the input size? Now, it is quite obvious when
we do arithmetic by hand, the kind of arithmetic we do in school that we do not go by magnitude.
We go by the number of digits when we do arithmetic such as addition with carrying we write down
the numbers in columns and then we add them column by column. So, the number of digits
determines how many columns we have to add. The same is true with subtraction or addition
or multiplication or long division and so on. So, clearly it is the number of digits which matters
and the number of digits is actually the same as the log. If we have numbers written in base 10,
then if we have a 6 digit number its log is going to be 5 points something.
And we get to log 6 we will have a 7 digit number and so on. So, the number of digits is
directly proportional to the log and so we can think of the log of the number as the input
size. So, this is a special case. So, for arithmetic functions involving numbers it is not the
number itself which is the input size, but the size of the number as expressed in how many digit
it takes us to write down the number. Now, the other thing we mentioned this is that we are going
to ignore constants. We are going to look at these functions in terms of orders of bandwidth.
That is the function grow as n and square and cube and so on. So, one justification for this is
because we are ignoring the notion of a basic operation or rather we are being a bit vague about
it. So, let us look at an example. So, supposing we originally consider our basic operations to be
assignments to variables or comparisons between variables. Now, we decide that we will include
swapping two values exchanging the contents of x and y as a basic operation. Now, one of the
first things we learn in programming is that in order to do this we need to go via temporary variable.
So, in order to exchange x and y in most programming languages you have to first save x in the
temporary variable then copy y to x and then restore y from the temporary variable. This takes three
assignments. So, if we take swap as a basic operation in our language as compared to a calculation
where we only look at assignments we are going to collapse three assignments into one basic
operation. So, there is a factor of three difference between how we would account for the
operations if we account for swap as a single operation. So, in order to get away from worrying
about these factors of three and two and so on one important way to do this is to just ignore
these constants when we are doing this calculation. So, that is another motivation for only looking at
what does it not look like. So, let us come back to this notion of worst case. So, as we said
we are really looking at all inputs of size n and among these inputs which inputs drive the
algorithm to take the maximum amount of time. So, let us look at a simple algorithm here which
is looking for a value k in an unsorted array a. So, in an unsorted array we have no idea where
the value k can be. So, the only thing we can do is swap from beginning to end.
So, we start by initializing this index i which is a position to 0 and then we have a loop
which says so long as we have not found the array element. So, long as a i is not k be increment
right we move to the next element. So, this is the loop and when we exit this loop there are one
or two possibilities either we have found the element in which case i is less than n.
What we have not found the element in which case i is become n. So, we check whether i is less
than n if i is less than n then we have found it and if i is bigger than n that means it is
not found. So, this is a simple algorithm. So, now in this algorithm the bottleneck is this loop
right. So, this can take up to n iterations. Now, when will it take n iterations that is the
worst case right. So, the worst case in this particular algorithm is it must go to the end either
if the last element is k or more generally if there is no copy of k in the array right. If there
is no k in the array we have to scan all the elements to determine that k does not exist right.
So, this becomes our worst case input. So, it is important to be able to look at an algorithm
and try to reconstruct what input would drive it to take the maximum amount of time. So, in this
simple case this simple example we can see that a case which forces us to execute the entire
loop can be generated by choosing a value of k which is not in the array. And in this case therefore,
the worst case is proportional to the size of the array n. But the crucial thing to remember is
that you know the determine which is the worst case input we have to understand the algorithm and
look at it. We cannot just blindly determine what is the worst case without knowing the problem at
the different algorithms we have to come up with different worst cases depending on what the
algorithm is supposed to do and how the algorithm is constructed. So, the worst case input is a
function of the algorithm itself. Now, we could look at a different measure right. So,
supposing we do not look at the worst case we say look at the average case. So, look at all
possible inputs and then try to see how much time it takes on each of these inputs and somehow
average it out right. Now, mathematically in order to compute this kind of an average we need to have
a good way of estimating what are all the possible inputs to a problem right. So, in although
this sounds like a very attractive motion in many programs is very difficult. So, supposing we are
doing the airline route problem right how do we consider this space of all possible route maps
and what is a difficult route map and so on right. So, what are we going to average over are all
these inputs equally likely. So, we need to look at probabilities and it is very often very difficult
to estimate the probabilities of different types of inputs. So, though it would make more sense
from the point of view of the behavior of the algorithm in practical situations to look at the
average case that is how does it behave over a space of inputs. In practice it is very hard to do
this because we cannot really quantify the space of possible inputs and assign them with meaningful
probabilities. So, to summarize we look at worst case even though it could be unrealistic
because the average case is hard if not impossible to complete. There are very limited situations where
it is possible to do an average case analysis but these are very very rare. So, the good thing about
a worst case analysis is if we can prove a good upper bound saying that even in the worst case this
algorithm performs efficiently then we have got a useful piece of information about the algorithm
that is it always works well. On the other hand if we find out that this algorithm has a bad
worst case upper bound we may have to look a little further how rare is this worst case as it
often arise in practice what type of inputs are worst case are they inputs that we will typically
see are there any simplifying assumptions that we can make which will rule out these worst cases
and so on. So, the worst case analysis is not a perfect way of doing it it is something which
is mathematically practical it is something that we can kind of hope to compute so that is one good
reason for doing it so that we can actually come up with a quantitative estimate and secondly it
does give us some useful information even though in some situations it may not be the most
realistic situation that we are likely to come across in practice.
